judgments.title: Suruhanjaya Sekuriti Malaysia v Tey Por Yee & ors
judgments.catchwords: KEYWORDS : SC v TEY POR YEE & 4 OTHERS Statutory Enforcement & Authority – Locus standi, regulatory enforcement, market regulator, public interest, statutory standing, relevant requirement, statutory pathway – Whether the Securities Commission has the statutory standing to institute civil enforcement proceedings under Section 200 and Section 360 of the CMSA 2007 to recover losses caused to public listed companies – Whether the narrow interpretation of "relevant requirement" for private aggrieved persons under Section 360(13)(c) restricts the regulator’s broader enforcement mandate under Section 360(13)(a). Corporate Fraud & Financial Malfeasance – Siphoning of funds, architecture of deceit, corporate schemes, master mind, nominee directors, shell companies, asset-less conduits, sham circular money trails – Whether the defendants collectively orchestrated and executed systematic corporate schemes to fraudulently siphon out fundraising capital (term loans, private placements, rights issues, ICULS) from the four listed public entities – Can a subsequent Board of Directors' ratification purge an antecedent statutory breach regarding the diversion of public funds? – Does statutory liability attach to de facto directors or shadow officers orchestrating fraud through fictitious agreements? – Does acting under third-party superior orders or executing bank transfers as a sole signatory without independent verification (wilful blindness) absolve a defendant from personal statutory liability? Securities Regulation & Statutes – Capital Markets and Services Act 2007 (CMSA), Section 179 (fraudulent device/scheme), Section 200 (civil proceedings gateway), Section 317A (causing wrongful loss), Section 360 (restraints and restitution orders). Civil Procedure & Defences – Limitation period, time bar, laches, prejudice due to delay, standard of proof (balance of probabilities), dual-track regimes, third-party superior orders, wilful blindness, de facto directors – Limitation of Action – Whether the Securities Commission’s cause of action is legally time-barred by a statutory limitation period, given that the underlying fraudulent events occurred more than seven years prior to the filing of the suit – Equity & Procedural Delay (Laches) – Whether the equitable defense of laches applies, and whether the defendants suffered substantial evidentiary or personal prejudice due to the regulator's delay in initiating legal proceedings. Constitutional & Remedial Law – Prosecutorial discretion, Public Prosecutor (Article 145(3) Federal Constitution), statutory remedies, civil penalty, restitution orders (joint and several liability), barring order – Constitutional Separation of Powers – Whether the Securities Commission’s pursuit of civil declarations, civil penalties, and restitutionary remedies constitutes an impermissible enforcement of criminal law that usurps the exclusive prosecutorial discretion of the Public Prosecutor under Article 145(3) of the Federal Constitution - Quantum and Remedies – What appropriate statutory remedies should be ordered under the CMSA, including civil penalties, barring orders, and the parameters for ordering restitution on a joint and several basis against the liable defendants. Statutory Interpretation – Purposive approach, Interpretation Acts 1948 and 1967 (Section 17A), legislative scheme, statutory text ambiguity.
judgments.judge: YA Dato' Indera Mohd Arief Emran Bin Arifin

judgments.title: SIVACHANDRAN A/L S JAYARAJAH v Pendakwa Raya
judgments.catchwords: Review jurisdiction - Rule 137 of the Rules of the Federal Court 1995 -Inherent powers of Federal Court – All sentences passed to be in accordance with the law – Avoiding miscarriage of justice - Exceptional circumstances - Fresh evidence of prisoner’s death following whipping. Constitutional Law - Federal Constitution - Articles 5(1), 8(1) and 8(2) Fundamental liberties - Life and personal liberty - Human dignity - Equal protection of the law - Whether it is in violation of medical ethics for medical officer to be participate in the execution of whipping. Judicial whipping - Corporal punishment - Whether judicial whipping amounts to cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment (“CIDT”) - Whether punishment of whipping is inconsistent with constitutional protection of life, dignity and bodily integrity. Whether whipping is disproportionate and therefore contrary to Article 8(1) - Whether exemption of women from whipping constitutes prohibited discrimination on ground only of gender is contrary to Art 8(2) - Intelligible differentia. Whether whipping is against Art. 5 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (“UDHR”) and the ASEAN Human Rights Declaration in its prohibitions against CIDT - Whether whipping is against customary international law.
